title: Mere Learning is Not Enough
body:
Mere Learning is Not Enough

न कर्तृत्वं न कर्माणि लोकस्य सृजति प्रभुः ।
न कर्मफलसंयोगं स्वभावस्तु प्रवर्तते ।।

"Neither the sense of doer-ship nor the nature of actions comes from God; nor does He create the fruits of actions. All this is enacted by the modes of material nature (guṇas). (Gita V-14)"

Following the death of Bharadwaja, the curse laid upon Raibhya found its tragic fulfillment. Raibhya's sons, Paravasu and Arvavasu, were highly educated Vedic scholars. One night, while Paravasu was walking through the dark forest to attend King Brihadyumna's grand sacrifice, he saw a shadow moving in the bushes. Mistaking it for a wild beast, he shot an arrow, only to discover that he had killed his own father, Raibhya, who was walking clad in deer skins.
Terrified of the sin of patricide (Brahmahatya), Paravasu begged his younger brother, the pure-hearted Arvavasu, to take upon himself the expiatory forest penances while he completed the King's sacrifice. Arvavasu, moved by fraternal love, agreed and spent years performing the rigorous purification rites. When Arvavasu returned to the sacrificial hall to join his brother, Paravasu, corrupted by jealousy, loudly proclaimed: 'This man is a sinner who has committed patricide; how can he enter this holy sacrificial ground?'
Arvavasu was unjustly expelled by the guards. He retired to the forest, performing intense penances dedicated to the Sun God, who eventually appeared and vindicated his innocence. The story demonstrates that scriptural learning (shastras) is a superficial garment unless it is digested into active, lived moral virtue. Paravasu possessed the intellectual knowledge of the Vedas but lacked the basic purity of heart, whereas the humble Arvavasu lived the true spirit of Dharma through selfless sacrifice.
